title: Hosea and Gomer
lead: Hosea's marriage to Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and the three children named Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi, are the first and best-known of the book's pictures of the LORD and Israel. Whether the marriage was an actual event, a vision or a story, what Gomer was when Hosea married her and whether the woman of chapter 3 is the same person have been argued from the Talmud to the present.

sections.b: A real marriage: the common view in modern commentaries, with debate on whether Gomer was already a prostitute, a woman in the Baal cult, or an ordinary woman who would later be unfaithful. A vision or parable: Maimonides and the Targum (the medieval commentators Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Kimhi are often reported on this question, but this site has not checked them, so none is placed in either camp). The Talmud (Pesachim 87a-b) takes it as real and puns on the names. The views on the woman of chapter 3 are: Gomer after leaving or being sold; a second woman; or the same event told in the first person.

sections.h: The woman in Hosea 2 and the feminist critique
sections.b: From the 1980s scholars such as Setel, Weems and Yee have argued that the picture of a husband stripping and shaming his wife makes violence against women a picture of God. Defenders (Ortlund, Keefe, Kelle, Moughtin-Mumby) reply that it is a metaphor aimed at Israel's leaders, that the threats are not commands and that the speech ends in restoration (2:14-23).
